John's memoir narrative describes Beryl's death occurring at Trudy and Mike Remy's Sacramento home (stroke following cancer surgery; coma; John present, authorized DNR). DOD remains 1998-08-01 per authoritative records.
Signature phrase: 'I smell the Villach' — coined on the road to an officers' vacation resort in Okinawa ~1952-53, referring to open sewers in Okinawan villages. Became a family catchphrase.
Adapted Golden Rule: 'Do unto others as dey been doin' to you.'
Ray + Dradie (her parents) celebrated 50th wedding anniversary at the Pasco Grange.
Secretary to U.S. Congressman Floyd Hicks in Olympia after graduating high school at 15.

John was the sole family member at the hospital when Beryl died; he authorized the DNR.
Would have been 100 years old on Christmas Day 2019 — confirming birth date Dec 25, 1919.
Born and raised on a farm in Lynden, Washington, the second oldest of six.
Graduated from high school when she was 15.
Moved to Olympia to work as secretary for Congressional Representative Floyd Hicks.
Moved into personnel management for the last years of her career.
John was at her bedside when she passed away and said the greatest regret of his life is that he failed to tell her one more time how much he loved her.
Signature phrase coined on the road to an officers' vacation resort in Okinawa: 'I smell the Villach!' — referring to open sewers in Okinawan villages. Became a family catchphrase.
Beryl's cousin Ralph Allen visited her years ago to share his family history findings.

Beryl rose by 5 a.m., could cook equally well on gas, electric, wood stove or campfire, and said pie a la mode was the best breakfast because it had fruit, dairy and starch; John called his father 'the Hammer' and her 'the Velvet Glove'.

Beryl was an adventurous cook who tried out dishes on her family, from pig's feet and liver to lima beans and okra. John called her about the world's best cook, with an almost endless list of desserts.
After George Sr. died, Beryl had his Lynx golf clubs re-gripped and gave them, with all his golf gear, to John.
Beryl was Nana to her grandsons Brian and Brendan (with George Sr. as Papa).
After Papa died, Nana went to Hawaii (Maui and Oahu) with John, Barbara, the boys, and Granny and Pops McKeldin.
Nana and Papa had many apple trees in their front yard; Papa made cider and Nana made apple pies.
milestones: Moved to Olympia to work for a Congressional Representative

During WWII Beryl first followed George to his training posts, then lived with her family in Pasco while he served in Hawaii; she lived in Pasco again with the children in 1952 while he went ahead to Okinawa.
Married Bob Shriver (m. after 1980); they lived on a golf course in Olympia, Washington
Married George Francis Adams Sr. (m. 9 Jan 1942, Pasco, Franklin County, Washington; licence Thurston County, 8 Jan 1942)
education: Beryl was an elementary school student of Amy Kulp and Alice Burk in Whatcom County.
career: Beryl went back to work when John was a high school freshman, starting as an administrative assistant to senior Army officers. (about 1961-1962)

Open question: Were Beryl and her younger siblings born in Whatcom County, and was Glen born somewhere other than the Lynden area? Irma asks to be corrected [Family research emails, email 48]
A street in the Pasco area laid out by her father Ray Simons is named after Beryl. [John Howard Adams, A Memoir, text line 591]
Beryl claimed her favorite pieces of chicken were the back and neck, which John believed was because nobody else wanted them and she hated to waste food. [John Howard Adams, A Memoir, text line 3273]

She and George took out the licence at Olympia on 8 Jan 1942, a month after Pearl Harbor, and married the next day at the Episcopal Church of Our Saviour in Pasco, where Beryl's parents lived; she was 22, and the church register names her parents Raymond and Dradie Simons (county marriage records; Episcopal Diocese of Spokane church records, vol. 2).

No street named Beryl appears on the present map of Pasco or the Tri-Cities, though her mother's name survives in West Dradie Street and Dradie Place and her brother's in Glen Acres; the street John remembers may have been renamed or absorbed when the land was redeveloped (OpenStreetMap, 2026).
